content: Spiracles are small openings located on the surface of certain animals, which typically connect to their respiratory systems. In elasmobranchs, such as sharks and rays, a spiracle is situated behind each eye. This structure is often utilized to pump water over the gills when the animal is at rest (Fouts, 2003). Primitive bony fishes, such as the bichir, also possess spiracles. In insects and some advanced spiders, spiracles are present on their exoskeletons and serve as entry points for air into the tracheal system (Solomon et al., 2002). However, the functionality of the tracheal system differs between these groups. In insects, the tracheal tubes primarily deliver oxygen directly to the tissues of the body. The spiracles can be opened and closed efficiently to minimize water loss. This process is regulated by the contraction of specialized muscles surrounding the spiracle. When the muscle relaxes, the spiracle opens. The closer muscle is under the control of the central nervous system but can also respond to localized chemical stimuli. Aquatic insects often possess similar or alternative mechanisms to prevent water from entering the tracheal system. In spiders, oxygen diffuses from the spiracles into the hemolymph, the circulatory fluid of these animals (Foelix, 1996). A comparable diffusion process is observed in some insect caterpillars. In these groups, respiration bears a closer resemblance to lung function. In spiders and other arachnids, for instance, specialized structures known as book lungs facilitate gas exchange.
